title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital 10 days after failed execution
description: Image source, ReutersByGrace Eliza GoodwinUpdated 5 hours agoUS death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched
body: Image source, ReutersByGrace Eliza GoodwinUpdated 5 hours agoUS death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.Pike, 50, has been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years and is continuing to receive medical care, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.She survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition.Pike regained consciousness earlier this week and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.Her case is now in uncharted territory as she is thought to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.Pike's lawyers said in their statement that she was "grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances".It is unclear what medical care Pike is receiving now that she is back in prison but her lawyers previously said she faced a "long road to recovery". The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.Figure caption, How widely used is the death penalty in the US?At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he did not know whether the state intends to try to execute her again.The judge ordered the state to preserve all evidence related to the failed injections. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.Shipp was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years. Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Tennessee Governor Bill Lee declined to block the execution. Since it failed, Pike's lawyers have renewed their calls for her sentence to be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and ShippPike lost consciousness and was taken to a local hospital following her botched execution. Her legal team believed for days that she was brain dead and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment.Pike eventually woke up and began talking again on Tuesday - her lawyer Randy Spivey said her first words were "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"At a press conference on Wednesday, her lawyers said she was shackled to the bed and suffering from pneumonia and significant swelling on her arms, while also being unable to swallow."We don't know the toll all of this will take" Spivey said of her mental health, adding that Pike felt "angry and confused".

schema.headline: Christa Pike discharged from hospital 10 days after failed execution

title: Three men found guilty of murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico
description: Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in
body: Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.The men's full names could not be given for legal reasons, and they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús. They are yet to be sentenced - but are likely to spend the rest of their lives in a prison.Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".During the trial in the northern Baja California state, the court heard that the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area. Their bodies were later found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.Robinson and her husband Martin have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial, and delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments before Friday's verdict."It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin said. Family members of Carter Rhoad joined the trial by video link.Robinson told reporters outside court a week ago that the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us".During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants.In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them.At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to honour the men by paddling out at a popular surfing spot and throwing flowers into the sea.Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.Amid the demands for action, state Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence."Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world," she said. "I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time."

schema.headline: Three men found guilty of murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico

title: Twelve killed in attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport
description: At least 12 people have been killed and 309 injured in an attack on an international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, local authorities say, days
body: At least 12 people have been killed and 309 injured in an attack on an international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, local authorities say, days after Yemen's Houthis claimed to have carried out similar strikes on the hub.The Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said the victims were four Saudi and two Bangladeshi nationals, while Egypt, Jordan, Palestine, Sudan, Syria and the US each had one of their citizens killed. Operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh have been suspended.More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing to the airport, according to news agency Reuters, citing an eyewitness. The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks", urging Americans to avoid the area.A projectile also fell near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam in eastern Saudi Arabia, the Saudi-led coalition which is fighting the Houthis said.The attack comes a day after authorities said three Saudis including a pilot were killed in two attacks on the airport by the Iran-backed Houthis the day prior. Another three people were killed in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.An eyewitness who said they had been in the domestic terminal told the news agency that they had seen gate 401 hit and "injured [people] in front of my eyes", adding: "Everyone was running."Western embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens away from the airport, while the UK Foreign Office told British nationals to stay away "until the airport is secure and to monitor the advice of the Saudi authorities".Several Gulf airlines said they had cancelled their flights to and from the airport, with Kuwait Airways citing the "security situation" there.All flights to Riyadh have either been diverted or cancelled, aviation tracker Flightradar shows.Doctors had been asked to report to hospitals to address the situation, a medical source told AFP."We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'," the medical source told the agency.The suspected attack comes during a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.The Houthis say they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.But the informal truce began to unravel in July.The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they described as a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

schema.headline: Twelve killed in attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport

title: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'
description: Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unaccept
body: Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague."Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu."If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure María Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president.Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway". He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year.

schema.headline: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'

title: 'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal
description: US President Donald Trump has said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" as he responded to Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of the U
body: US President Donald Trump has said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" as he responded to Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of the US diesel deal with Russia.The Ukrainian president warned a new deal to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against his nation, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday that Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries."He'd better damn well stop," Trump said, before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".Global fuel supplies, including diesel, have been severely limited by the war against Iran launched by the US and Israel, which led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil products usually flows.Russia - a major producer - and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes on each other's energy infrastructure and transport facilities, further straining energy markets."We said, 'you can do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries', because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump continued."He could have made many deals and for some reason, he never does."Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev described Trump's intervention as "iconic and historic", saying that Ukraine "needs leadership actually focused on peace".The US president confirmed on Friday that an agreement had been reached with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April.Zelensky reacted by saying it would allow Moscow to raise new funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.He also accused Moscow of taking the deal "to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they keep dropping bombs on cities" following deadly new strikes on Zaporizhzhia.The Ukrainian president spoke to several allies on Saturday to discuss the latest developments, calling for "real decisions to protect lives in Ukraine" and to protect European security.A Downing Street spokesperson said UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had spoken to Zelensky and offered his "complete solidarity".The pair had agreed Russia should acquiesce to "an immediate energy ceasefire" and end its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea, the spokesperson said, as "this would immediately release more energy and food supplies into the global market".News of the US-Russia diesel deal was also met with criticism by EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas, who echoed Zelensky in saying that suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.The deal with Russia is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.The average price of diesel is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA – up from last month's $5.94 average, and $3.68 last year.Under the deal, Russia would release an initial 300,000 tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace" followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November.A further million would follow, Trump wrote on Truth Social, and then another 3m tonnes "within a short period of time" – but he noted that this delivery will be "based on the condition of their diesel refineries".In the past 10 months, Russia experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country due to Ukrainian drones strikes on its oil refineries.Diesel production in Russia dropped by an estimated 30%, according to the International Energy Agency.Trump had already called for new elections in Ukraine last December, external, saying Ukrainian voters should have the choice to replace Zelensky.Since the war broke out in 2022 Ukraine has been under martial law, meaning elections are suspended.

schema.headline: 'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal

title: Four dead and thousands without power after Hurricane Isaias lashes US
description: Figure caption, Watch: Florida thrashed as Hurricane Isaias makes landfallByMadeline HalpertReporting fromNew YorkUpdated 1 hour agoFour people have d
body: Figure caption, Watch: Florida thrashed as Hurricane Isaias makes landfallByMadeline HalpertReporting fromNew YorkUpdated 1 hour agoFour people have died and hundreds of thousands are without power after Hurricane Isaias battered parts of the southern US with powerful winds and heavy rain. Officials reported two deaths each in the states of Alabama and Florida, which included people who were killed when trees fell on their houses. At least 600,000 people were without power in several states as of Saturday afternoon, according to tracker PowerOutage. Isaias made landfall in Florida late on Friday with maximum sustained winds of 105mph (168km/h) before being downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone. The storm felled trees and ripped the roofs off buildings. Alabama, Florida and Georgia all declared states of emergency ahead of its arrival, while both Florida and Alabama issued mandatory evacuation orders to thousands of people.Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon is bearing down on Mexico's Pacific coast and has strengthened to category four. It is expected to make landfall sometime overnight.And Tropical Storm Rachel, also in the Pacific Ocean, is edging towards land and is expected to hit southern California later on Saturday.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The roof was blown off an apartment complex in Milton, FloridaImage source, Getty ImagesTwo deaths related to Isaias were reported in Florida's Escambia County. A woman was killed when a tree fell on her house, local Sheriff Chip Simmons said. Joey Williams told NewsNation his wife had died in the storm. He said they went outside to snap pictures of the damage but, when they went back into their home, a tree fell through the roof and trapped them. "I was able to squeeze out. My wife didn't make it," Williams told the outlet. Simmons later reported that a man had died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a garage that was not properly ventilated. Four other people who were in the same house were taken to hospital. Officials had to rescue people in vehicles that became submerged by floodwaters. The Florida National Guard shared pictures of a truck stuck in a flood ditch, saying soldiers "stopped, swam to the vehicle and pulled its occupants to safety".Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said flooding was a continued risk and warned of a "very hazardous situation". Image source, EPAImage caption, In Florida, the storm tore through housesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The canopy of a petrol station collapsed in Gulf Breeze, FloridaIn neighbouring Alabama, a sheriff was injured when a tree fell on him as he was responding to a car crash. "Unfortunately, we have also learned that two Alabamians have lost their lives," Governor Kay Ivey said in a post on X, without giving further details on the circumstances of the deaths.She also said officials were concerned about "spinoff tornadoes" in the state from the strong winds and heavy rain. "As we approach the weekend and any travel plans, make sure you have reliable information as conditions develop," she said.In Charleston, South Carolina, officials asked people to stay home on Saturday night as high tide is expected to reach 7.5ft (2.3m). "After dark, floodwater is much harder to see and it's impossible to judge how deep it is from behind the wheel," the city said. The storm is expected to continue to weaken as it travels to the north-east, but the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) warned that the Carolinas and Georgia could see floods from up to 10 inches (25cm) of rainfall. Hurricane Isaias was the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.Image source, EPAImage caption, Residents have begun removing felled treesFigure caption, Watch: Powerful waves crash ashore as Hurricane Isaias approaches US

schema.headline: Four dead and thousands without power after Hurricane Isaias lashes US

title: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
description: Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the pa
body: Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

schema.headline: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres

title: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
description: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legi
body: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear. It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy"."Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked."Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

schema.headline: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices

title: CJP at Jantar Mantar: 'Cockroach' group says leaders detained at Delhi protest
description: Hundreds of protesters have been detained in Delhi during the latest demonstration by the Gen-Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) calling for electoral
body: Hundreds of protesters have been detained in Delhi during the latest demonstration by the Gen-Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) calling for electoral reforms.The group said its founder Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - was detained with other leaders shortly after landing in Delhi. Tens of thousands of security personnel were deployed and roads barricaded ahead of the demonstration, though the CJP insisted it would go ahead.Delhi Police has not commented on the detentions, but had refused permission for the protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital.The group - who are not registered as a political party in India - are seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.Under Kumar's leadership, India's election commission has undertaken a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - it said this was a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.But in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.Before arriving in Delhi, the CJP's founder Dipke said: "If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail or trying to intimidate us with the fear of imprisonment, you are mistaken."He and and two other leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained on their flight from Mumbai on Saturday. The group claimed the three men have been taken to an undisclosed location. Delhi Police have not commented.Ajinkya Shinde, the CJP's new designated leader while the others are in detention, released a video telling protesters that "if Delhi Police tries to stop you, wherever they stop you will become your Jantar Mantar".Student activist Neha Bora, who had also been detained by Delhi Police, urged demonstrators to "hold the line".The large number of protesters expected to descend on Delhi were unable to get anywhere close to Jantar Mantar due to the heavy security presence and road blocks.Announcements could be heard across the city, asking people to co-operate with the police.One protester, Sabika Muzaffar, told the BBC she and her mother expected to be detained. "On the way to the protest site, instead of reciting hymns and verses as we usually do, my mother and I were rote learning our lawyer's number," she said.She said that showing up to protest was "her way of defending the country and its democracy". A few minutes after Muzaffar spoke to the BBC she was taken away by police.Several trains to and from major Delhi stations had been cancelled and dozens of metro stations were closed from Friday night.Buses packed with detained protesters were seen being driven away from the protest site.

schema.headline: CJP at Jantar Mantar: 'Cockroach' group says leaders detained at Delhi protest

title: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he would not watch it
description: JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution.The US vice-president expressed uncertainty to reporters about
body: JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution.The US vice-president expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the December execution would go ahead as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen". He added that "if it's through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it".Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but said the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.Nidal Hasan killed 13 unarmed soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009 and injured another 32. His execution would be the first military firing squad execution in more than 60 years.The Pentagon announced its desire to execute the former US Army major by firing squad over the attack on 3 December earlier this week.US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth then said the execution would be livestreamed for the public, as "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".Trump was asked about the possibility that visuals of Hasan's execution could be used as propaganda for terrorists as he left the White House on Friday.Calling Hasan "totally nuts", he replied: "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."The Pentagon declined to comment further when asked for more information about a decision on the livestream. Vance condemned Hasan's attack on the base as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11" while speaking to reporters on Friday.Asked about how his Catholic faith affected his stance on the plan to stream a public execution, Vance questioned whether it would happen. But he noted that Hasan, a military psychiatrist, was meant to treat soldiers for mental illness and other problems, but had instead "took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived". The possible livestreaming of the execution has been met with criticism from both political parties. Republican Senator John Curtis pointed to Rome's history of a "bloody spectacle" corrupting people who watched, warning that public executions eroded civilisations "when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment".Curtis said that Hegseth's plan "risks feeding that appetite" and urged him to reconsider. "The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent."Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group.Georgia lawmaker Austin Scott, a Republican, said that while he "absolutely" supported the death sentence, livestreaming executions was "what jihadists do - America is better than that".John Bolton, a former national security adviser during the first Trump administration, told BBC's Radio 4 PM that he supported capital punishment, but that the livestream was "unnecessary" because there were provisions for interested parties to view the execution in person."I just think this is a mark by Secretary Hegseth doing something he thinks will please President Trump," he said. "I think that's really not appropriate for a secretary of defence."The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also condemned the decision to publicly livestream Hasan's execution, expressing "shock and great sorrow".The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture".All of the social media platforms the US government has accounts on have prohibitions in place on violent images and videos, as well as those that show death or glorify or make a spectacle of violence.Meta - owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads - explicitly bans any livestream of capital punishment. YouTube bans all "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers", while TikTok similarly bars "extremely graphic, violent or disturbing content" that includes the "moment of someone's death" and "the shooting of an individual".But both YouTube and TikTok make exceptions in instances of "public interest".Asked whether a livestream of an execution qualifies for the exception if it is government-sanctioned, a TikTok spokeswoman said: "Regardless, I'd point you back to the not allowed section which reflects our approach."The policy at X, which has loosened content moderation since billionaire Elon Musk took over the platform, prohibits content "glorifying" violence.Meta, YouTube and X did not respond to multiple BBC requests for comment.

schema.headline: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he would not watch it

title: Ukraine war: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 20 people
description: Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 20 people including four children, local officials said
body: Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 20 people including four children, local officials said.The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the southern city on Saturday morning. At least 32 others were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks on Zaporizhzhia were Russia expressing "its thanks" for a deal announced by US President Donald Trump last night easing sanctions on Moscow to import Russian diesel.He added that 13 other regions had come under attack overnight, arguing this demonstrated Russia took "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting".Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes in Zaporizhzhia show an apartment block mostly destroyed. "The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Harchenko told Ukrainian television from the scene. She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day. The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble.Harchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city."Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles.Zelensky was quick to criticise Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Analysts view the deal as an attempt by the US president to allay domestic concerns about high fuel prices ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.Zelensky wrote on social media on Saturday that Russian attacks on energy facilities in the capital, Kyiv, demonstrated Russia's "true intentions"."Russia's choice is war. And they will be ready to end it only when they feel that their ability to drag the war out is diminishing."Unfortunately, the signals Russia received yesterday were entirely different – signals suggesting that it could simply keep attacking. And this needs to be corrected."Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as Moscow's full-scale invasion, launched in 2022, drags on.On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region. The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv.The number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55%, external in the first eight months of this year, according to the UN.Russia has also stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure as winter approaches, a strategy it has undertaken in previous years. Kyiv has repeatedly accused it of targeting Ukraine's civilian population, which Moscow denies.For its part, Ukraine has increasingly adopted a policy of striking infrastructure often deep inside Russia that is crucial to its economy, including several oil refineries and terminals.Several strikes on data centres owned by Yandex have left the tech giant struggling to maintain services.Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at curtailing revenue streams for Russia's war machine.

schema.headline: Ukraine war: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 20 people

title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
description: Image source, Swedish Coast GuardImage caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022BySarah Rainsford
body: Image source, Swedish Coast GuardImage caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022BySarah RainsfordEastern and Southern Europe correspondentSerhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.But German police were already closing in on him.After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".Both he and his country have denied any involvement.Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor It was 02:03 on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.Both have been inoperable ever since.Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.They went on following the forensic crumbs.Eventually they led to Ukraine.The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.The saboteursNone of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them."Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution."Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence."At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".Image source, Omar Marques/Getty ImagesImage caption, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from CroatiaGermany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.But he is a civilian.Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."Croatia is a different matter.Political ripplesThe implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further."I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.He argued that Nord Stream had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe. "Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."First in the dockSerhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot.He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.They are not saying, though.And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.

schema.headline: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine

title: Kenya's first Ebola case: Questions remain after man travelled across three nations undetected
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Nearly 70 potential contacts have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi ByWycliffe MuiaA Kenyan businessman was able
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Nearly 70 potential contacts have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi ByWycliffe MuiaA Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.DR CongoThe account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection. Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care. We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.UgandaHowever, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.Image source, EPAImage caption, The man's funeral was held under strict safety protocolsOnce he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.KenyaSimilarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.CDC adviceMankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival."When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.More from the BBC on the Ebola outbreak:

schema.headline: Kenya's first Ebola case: Questions remain after man travelled across three nations undetected

title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An estimated crowd of 20,000 gathered in Kentucky in 1936 for the public hanging of Rainey BetheaBySheila Fly
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An estimated crowd of 20,000 gathered in Kentucky in 1936 for the public hanging of Rainey BetheaBySheila FlynnSenior US reporterUpdated 10:17 BSTThey came in their thousands from near and far. Men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heatwave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to spectators.By the execution time of 05:00, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner". The local sheriff had died four months earlier and his widow had become his unlikely replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was a hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in the US. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.Image source, FPG/Staff/GettyImage caption, Men, women and children attended the hanging, which marked the last high-profile public execution in the USA little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad in December would be livestreamed."People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked."I never imagined [another] public execution," he told the BBC.He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining - it was at 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%."It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's likely that millions or more will tune in.With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment... bring your popcorn, invite your friends". Figure caption, Americans discuss their views on the death penalty after the botched execution in Tennessee of convicted murderer Christa PikeSonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream."What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up... to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's death in 2002, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution."I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."But the polarisation and rhetoric in US politics may have set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University."Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution - they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"Figure caption, Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed?Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong.Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said surveys point to a declining appetite for violence in the US."This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labelled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people.""I think it's this: a public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country."The debate over Hegseth's surprise announcement appeared to be playing out within the White House on Friday. US Vice-President JD Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the public execution would go ahead as planned and said he would not watch it if it were livestreamed.Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.He did not answer the question of whether he'd watch Hasan's execution. "I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

schema.headline: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?

title: France's school protests are about more than broken classrooms
description: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nationImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Hundreds of thousand
body: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nationImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Hundreds of thousands of students have protested across France since the end of last monthByNick BeakeEurope correspondentAs dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets."There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school."We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down."They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.Image caption, Massicella, second left, and her friends have been protesting in LilleThe protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country.Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.Figure caption, Watch: Marseille school students explain why they're protestingThe problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils)."It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.Image caption, Teachers, including Marine Monins and Marjorie Roussel, have joined their students in calling for changeOn Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country."It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest."It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police have been accused of heavy-handed tacticsThe unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth."For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.Image caption, Kaspar says strangers have been hijacking some protestsBut Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests."These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring."Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Marine Le Pen has condemned damage to schoolsThe protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise.More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country.But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape.The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant.Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration.Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race.Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Jean-Luc Mélenchon has been supportive of the demonstrationsJean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks.Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth.He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history.Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration."I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march.Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros.She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs.The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The 1968 protests have carved an indelible memory in French social historyThe problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix.This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago.Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve.And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically.What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess.The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase.Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace.She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils.For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Many students have said they will not back down from protestingBut many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition."In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris."That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit."As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped.But not for long.A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street."The canteen is still open."The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated.Additional reporting by Bruno Boelpaep and Manon Prat

schema.headline: France's school protests are about more than broken classrooms
